title: Patacara the teacher
hook: the woman who lost everything becomes a teacher of other grieving women

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uppalavanna, foremost in psychic power, who met Mara unafraid. Your line: she survived. Whose story did you see whole? Today, a survivor who turned around and taught. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

An arrow, lodged where nobody can see it. That's how a group of grieving mothers, in the verses of the elder nuns, speak of their sorrow for their children. And they name the woman who drew it out: Patacara. Her own losses are the part of her story tradition tells first: a husband, children, parents, all lost, tradition says, in a stretch of days so terrible that she wandered out of her mind with grief, until she reached the Buddha. That's usually where the telling stops. Today it keeps going. The woman who lost everything becomes the one other grieving women come looking for.
screen: `AN ARROW NO ONE CAN SEE.` → `SHE DREW IT OUT.` → `THE GRIEVING COME TO HER.`

segments.voice: First, her own waking. In her verses in the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, Patacara tells how she washed her feet and watched the water as it ran down the slope, and steadied her mind on it. The commentary adds what she saw: some water went a little way, some further, some further still, the way lives run short and long. That evening she took a lamp into her cell, sat on her bed, and drew down the wick with a needle. As the flame went out, her mind was freed. Second, what she says to the grieving. In another poem, grieving mothers remember what she told them. You don't know the way he came, she says, or the way he went. He came from somewhere unseen and went on somewhere unseen. So why weep, crying, my son? It sounds hard on paper. In the poem it lands as the voice of someone who stood in the same place. Third, what the women say back. In the verses, they tell how she drew out the arrow from their hearts, the grief for their children, and they go forth as nuns. Other nuns' verses name her too: they did as Patacara taught, washed their feet, went to their cells, and woke. Fourth, the title. In the list of foremost disciples, Patacara is named first among the nuns who know the discipline, the community's rules. The woman who once wandered wild with grief became the keeper of order. Grief didn't vanish. It became a way to recognize someone else's. From grief to teacher.
screen: `WATER DOWN A SLOPE, A LAMP GOES OUT.` · `HE CAME AND WENT UNSEEN.` · `SHE DREW OUT THE ARROW.` · `KEEPER OF THE DISCIPLINE.` · then, large: `FROM GRIEF TO TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help one person in grief. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is grieving now: a loss this year, or an old one that still sits close. Patacara didn't lead with answers. She sat down with people first. So just hold this person in mind, and ask what might actually help. A message. A meal. Their person's name, said out loud. Your company, with nothing to fix. Choose one thing, small and doable. Then let it rest, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Patacara the teacher. The woman who lost everything, woke watching a lamp go out, and became the teacher grieving women came to. Today's word.
Your line: from grief to teacher. Today, do the one small thing you chose for someone who is grieving, and keep it simple. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Patacara's verses and the verses of the women she taught are read in the Therigatha, and in Theravada communities her story is told as a teaching on grief and on how short and uncertain life is.

fork.setup: you're Patacara. a mother comes to you crying for her dead son. you've lost children too. what do you say?
options: tell her the pain will pass soon.
ask her: you don't know the way he came or went, so why cry 'my son'?
tell her to go home and rest.
fork.reveal: in the verses, she asks where the son came from and went, and the grieving women say she drew the arrow from their hearts.

original.note: Pali salla, a dart or arrow: the grieving women say Patacara drew it out.

trapdoor: what you thought: the woman who lost everything.
what it means: the woman who lost everything, woke, and became a teacher of grieving women.
what a scholar hears: Therigatha verses credit her with her own awakening and with teaching other nuns, and the Buddha's list names her foremost among nuns in the discipline.

notes: All paraphrased; Mrs. Rhys Davids's Psalms of the Sisters (1909) exists, but the writer was not certain of its wording.

Her losses are summarized and attributed to tradition (Dhammapada commentary, verses 113 and 288-289); the count of losses was left out on purpose. Check the hook's 'her own story is the one people tend to tell' reads as fair.

Confirm Thig 6.1 is the poem to grieving mothers ('you don't know the way he came or went') and the 'arrow drawn out' line, and that Thig 5.11 (the thirty nuns, number omitted) follows her instruction about washing feet and entering the cell.
Thig 5.10: confirm she drew down the wick 'with a needle' (pin).

Editor: hook no longer opens on a grieving mother with a dead son (day 760 opens on Kisa Gotami's dead child); it now opens on the arrow image from Thig 6.1, and 'the one people tend to tell' became 'the part tradition tells first'. The water running short, further and further still is from the Dhammapada commentary (v. 113), not her Therigatha verses, so it is now attributed to the commentary. Thig 6.1 is now framed as the mothers remembering her words, and the garbled 'Why cry out, my son?' was fixed.
